name: Code
title: Code
description: Execute custom code to transform data
whenToUse: Transform, reshape, compute or combine data inline with a JS expression: map or filter an array, build an object, derive a value from upstream outputs. Prefer it over routing data through an LLM node just to reformat or merge it, because it is deterministic and free. Toggle generateIds for content hashes, or saveToContext to keep the result reachable from later templates.

inputs.name: signal
inputs.description: Upstream data. Nothing is read from it directly: the `code` field's template reaches {{ signal.… }} and the engine resolves it before this node runs, so by the time the node executes the answer is already in config.

outputs.name: ids
outputs.description: { universalId, contentId } — only when Generate IDs is on

code.title: Code
code.description: JS expression to transform data. It is a template field, so the ENGINE evaluates it before this node runs and what arrives here is already the finished value. That is why this node makes no request and does no computing of its own beyond the optional id hashes.

generateIds.title: Generate IDs
generateIds.description: Also emit a universalId and a contentId derived from the value, for downstream dedup and ref hydration to join on.

saveToContext.title: Save to Context
saveToContext.description: Keep the value for the rest of this run, so a later node's template can reach it as {{ saved.<this node's id> }} without an edge.

authRequired.title: Require sign-in
authRequired.description: Only a signed-in caller may run this step. Leave off and it runs for whoever the workflow's trigger admitted, which is the usual answer.

authRole.title: Require role
authRole.description: A claim the caller's account must carry, as noun:verb (finance:approve, payments:refund). Leave blank to require only that they are signed in.

package.name: flow
package.packageFile:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/package.schema.json

# FLOW AS MANIFESTS, node by node.
#
# The one package that can migrate INCREMENTALLY, because it declares no credentials. The
# all-or-nothing rule that forced `aws-toolkit` and `cloudinary` to be split came entirely from
# the credential coexistence check (a node needs `credentials/<name>.yaml` in its own package,
# but that file alongside a code `registerCredential` is an error). With no credentials there is
# no conflict, and `src/index.ts` registers each node on its own line — so a node moves by
# writing its manifest and deleting those two lines.
#
# NO allowedHosts, and that is not an omission. Nothing in this package reaches the network at
# all; an empty list means the executor refuses every host, which is exactly right here.
#
# WHAT IS STILL CODE, and why:
#
#   UMAP  runs umap-js IN PROCESS. Genuine local compute, reaching no host. Also of doubtful
#         value as written: it received ONE vector, faked a second by copying it with +0.0001
#         on every element so umap-js would run, and returned near-meaningless coordinates —
#         the real reduction lives in services/umap now. A candidate for removal, undecided.
#
#   SendObject  RETIRED to _legacy, user decision 2026-07-29 — it published to the live
#               session rather than answering the graph, and the `publish` capability that
#               replaced that lane (see Suggestions) covers the need.
#
# Suggestions, which used to sit on this list for the same reason as SendObject, is now a
# manifest: what actually needed code was one push into the caller's template state, and that
# is the executor's `publish` capability (api/publish.yaml) — declared under `requires` below.
#
# AND ONE REMOVAL rather than a migration. Gone from the catalog, so a saved workflow naming
# it now fails to resolve the type:
#
#   MCP             a generic schema-driven mcpService provider from before real service nodes
#                   existed. Superseded by UnoverseMCP in the engine and by per-vendor providers
#                   (HubspotMCP, SalesforceMCP, SlackMCP), so nothing needed it.
#
# FieldValidator was on this list, removed because its five outputs all derive from one
# properties-map cascade and expressions had no way to bind an intermediate value — the cascade
# had to be written out again inside every expression needing it; `completionPercentage` alone
# came to four copies. Named helpers (shared/helpers.yaml) are exactly that binding, so it is
# BACK, same type and connectors, and any workflow that named it resolves again.

name: flow
displayName: Flow
description: Control flow, routing and workflow annotation
version: 2.0.0
category: flow
logoUrl: https://res.cloudinary.com/sonik/image/upload/v1751366180/gravity/icons/gravityIcon.png

features:
  - Notes and documentation on the canvas
  - Branch, relay and read the running workflow's own context
  - Transform data inline, with optional content ids and run-scoped saved values
  - Loop over an array, running real workflow steps once per item
  - Validate collected data against a schema and get the next missing field to ask for
  - Push suggested FAQs, actions and recommendations to the live chat UI

requires:
  # 1.7.0 for named helpers (shared/helpers.yaml), which FieldValidator's emit rows call —
  # the same floor spatial set when helpers landed. Previously 1.5.0.
  executorVersion: ">=1.7.0"
  # Code's "Save to Context" toggle. Declared even though it cannot silently no-op the way a cache
  # read can — an executor without `save` throws rather than shrugging — because the reason to
  # declare is the same either way: the package says which platform capabilities its nodes need, so
  # installing it against an older executor fails at install rather than at run.
  state:
    - save
  # The LoopStart/LoopEnd pair. More is at stake in declaring these than in most capabilities: an
  # executor that cannot keep an index does not iterate, so an install that skipped this check would
  # run a loop body exactly once and report success.
  loop:
    - open
    - read
    - advance
  # Suggestions' whole job. Declared because on an executor without the publish lane the node
  # would emit its connector and never reach the screen — "worked" everywhere except the one
  # place it matters.
  publish: true

shared.helpers.yaml:
# FLOW'S NAMED FUNCTIONS. FieldValidator's schema cascade and Suggestions' normalizer,
# because both nodes' whole job is shaping one object that several expressions then read.
#
# FieldValidator exists again BECAUSE of this file: it was retired rather than migrated when
# every one of its five outputs derived from the same properties-map cascade and, with no way
# to bind an intermediate value, the cascade had to be written out again inside every
# expression needing it — completionPercentage alone came to four copies. Named helpers are
# the capability that reversed that decision: the cascade runs here, once, and each emit row
# picks one field.
#
# A helper sees only its arguments and its siblings: no config, no credentials, no caller
# scope. Same sandbox as every other expression, no extra authority.

helpers:
  # WHERE THE FIELDS LIVE, across the three shapes the retired node accepted — transcribed
  # from its extractSchemaInfo, cases in the same order:
  #
  #   1. a minted TOOL schema      { inputSchema: { json: { properties, required } } }
  #   2. plain JSON Schema         { properties, required }
  #   3. a bare object             its keys ARE the fields, nothing is required
  #
  # All three still arrive in practice, because the schema is whatever the upstream wire
  # carries: an agent's tool definition, an authored form schema, or a hand-built object.
  schemaInfo:
    args: [schema]
    body: >-
      return (!schema || typeof schema !== 'object')
        ? { fieldNames: [], requiredList: [], propertiesMap: {} }
        : (((schema.inputSchema || {}).json || {}).properties
            ? { fieldNames: Object.keys(schema.inputSchema.json.properties),
                requiredList: schema.inputSchema.json.required || [],
                propertiesMap: schema.inputSchema.json.properties }
            : (schema.properties
                ? { fieldNames: Object.keys(schema.properties),
                    requiredList: schema.required || [],
                    propertiesMap: schema.properties }
                : { fieldNames: Object.keys(schema), requiredList: [], propertiesMap: schema }))

  # A field is MISSING when absent, null, or the empty string — the empty string because these
  # values come off forms and chat slots, where "" is what an unanswered question produces.
  # No data at all means everything is missing, not an error: the first turn of a slot-filling
  # conversation legitimately starts from nothing.
  missingFields:
    args: [fieldNames, data]
    body: >-
      return (!data || typeof data !== 'object')
        ? fieldNames
        : fieldNames.filter(f => data[f] == null || data[f] === '')

  # THE SUGGESTIONS OBJECT, normalized at the source — transcribed from the retired
  # Suggestions executor. The template's contract is `{ text }` (the SDK stores producer data
  # opaquely and knows no "faq", UNOVERSE_STATE_MODEL §8), while authors write a string,
  # `{ text }` or `{ question }` — so the flattening happens HERE and the SDK never has to.
  #
  # Per-key fallback, signal over config, exactly as the retired node resolved it: a workflow
  # usually wires the whole object off an upstream extractor, and static config is the
  # standing default for whichever keys the signal does not carry.
  #
  # The retired node's two-level "source node / output handle" probing is deliberately NOT
  # transcribed: that unwrapped the LEGACY engine's signal envelope, and the manifest executor
  # binds the payload by input port name instead — there is nothing left to unwrap.
  suggestionsOf:
    args: [given, authored]
    body: >-
      return ((sig) => ({
        faqs: ((sig.faqs || authored.faqs) || []).map(f => ({
          text: typeof f === 'string'
            ? f
            : ((f || {}).text != null ? f.text : ((f || {}).question != null ? f.question : ''))
        })),
        actions: (sig.actions || authored.actions) || [],
        recommendations: (sig.recommendations || authored.recommendations) || []
      }))(given || {})

  # ONE report with everything the node emits. `null` rather than `undefined` for an absent
  # next field, so the emit rows can test it with a plain comparison.
  #
  # NEXT-FIELD PRIORITY is the retired node's: first missing field that the schema marks
  # required, else first missing field in schema order — `filter(...)[0] || missing[0]`
  # collapses both cases because an empty filter yields undefined and falls through.
  fieldReport:
    args: [schema, data]
    body: >-
      return ((info) =>
        ((missing) =>
          ((next) => ({
            nextField: next,
            nextFieldSchema: (next == null || info.propertiesMap[next] == null)
              ? null
              : info.propertiesMap[next],
            missingFields: missing,
            isComplete: missing.length === 0,
            completionPercentage: info.fieldNames.length === 0
              ? 100
              : Math.round((info.fieldNames.length - missing.length) / info.fieldNames.length * 100)
          }))(missing.length === 0
            ? null
            : (missing.filter(f => info.requiredList.includes(f))[0] || missing[0]))
        )(helpers.missingFields(info.fieldNames, data))
      )(helpers.schemaInfo(schema))

files.api/events.yaml:
# NEITHER ROW READS `response`. There is no reply to read: the only entry in `run` is a state write,
# and the value it stores is the same one emitted here. Everything this node emits comes from
# `config`, because the engine's template resolver has already done the computing.
#
# THE HASHES ARE TRANSCRIBED from the retired node's hashUtils.ts, byte for byte, and they have to
# be: dedup and ref hydration downstream JOIN on these ids, so a different algorithm would not
# error, it would simply stop matching rows minted before today.
#
#   contentId    sha256 of the value, first 12 hex chars
#   universalId  sha256 of `<workflowId>-<nodeId>-<value>`, first 12
#
# `Object.keys(x).toSorted()` as a JSON.stringify replacer is the canonicalisation, and it is the
# reason `toSorted` was added to the sandbox. Without it the same object hashes differently depending
# on the order its keys happened to be built in. `toSorted` and not `sort`, because `sort` reorders
# its receiver in place and the receiver here is live run data.
#
# The `|| 'unknown'` and `|| 'code'` fallbacks are the retired node's, kept so a run missing an id
# hashes to what it always did rather than to the text "undefined".
#
# ONE DELIBERATE DIFFERENCE, and it only touches a case that used to crash. `createContentHash` fed
# its argument straight to `Object.keys`, which THROWS on null and undefined — so a Code node whose
# expression evaluated to null failed the workflow outright with a TypeError from inside a hash
# helper. Here an absent value hashes the empty string, which is what `createUniversalId` already did
# for the same case. Nothing that previously produced an id produces a different one.

- emit: output
  value: "return config.code"

- emit: ids
  when: "return !!config.generateIds"
  value: |
    return {
      universalId: sha256(
        config.code === undefined || config.code === null
          ? `${scope.workflowId || 'unknown'}-${scope.nodeId || 'code'}`
          : `${scope.workflowId || 'unknown'}-${scope.nodeId || 'code'}-${typeof config.code === 'string' ? config.code : JSON.stringify(config.code, Object.keys(config.code).toSorted())}`
      ).substring(0, 12),
      contentId: sha256(
        typeof config.code === 'string'
          ? config.code
          : (config.code === undefined || config.code === null
              ? ''
              : JSON.stringify(config.code, Object.keys(config.code).toSorted()))
      ).substring(0, 12)
    }
files.api/run.yaml:
# ONE ENTRY, AND IT REACHES NO HOST. `state: save` is platform storage, so this node still makes no
# request — which is the whole point of it, since the value it emits was computed by the engine's
# template resolver before the node was even entered.
#
# GATED, so the entry leaves no trace when the toggle is off: a skipped call records no
# `calls.saved` key, and the `__saveToContext` flag on the output envelope is derived from exactly
# that. Both halves of "save to context" therefore turn on and off together, which they must —
# writing the value without the flag makes it reachable from the NEXT node and not this one.
#
# NO `key`, and lint refuses one. The saved-context hash is `saved:<executionId>` with one field per
# node, and that layout belongs to the engine: its resolver reads the key when building a template
# scope and the run deletes it at the end. A manifest addressing it by hand would also have the
# deployment namespace applied to the one key that must not carry it, and the write would land where
# nothing looks — silently, with the toggle still appearing to work.

- name: saved
  when: "return !!config.saveToContext"
  state: save
  value: "return config.code"
files.config.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/config.schema.json

configSchema:
  type: object
  required: [code]
  properties:
    code:
      type: object
      title: Code
      description: >-
        JS expression to transform data. It is a template field, so the ENGINE evaluates it before
        this node runs and what arrives here is already the finished value. That is why this node
        makes no request and does no computing of its own beyond the optional id hashes.
      default: ""
      "ui:field": template
    generateIds:
      type: boolean
      title: Generate IDs
      description: >-
        Also emit a universalId and a contentId derived from the value, for downstream dedup and
        ref hydration to join on.
      default: false
      "ui:widget": toggle
    saveToContext:
      type: boolean
      title: Save to Context
      description: >-
        Keep the value for the rest of this run, so a later node's template can reach it as
        {{ saved.<this node's id> }} without an edge.
      default: false
      "ui:widget": toggle
"ui:order": [code, generateIds, saveToContext]
files.interface.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/interface.schema.json

inputs:
  - name: signal
    type: object
    description: >-
      Upstream data. Nothing is read from it directly: the `code` field's template reaches
      {{ signal.… }} and the engine resolves it before this node runs, so by the time the node
      executes the answer is already in config.
    required: false

outputs:
  - name: output
    type: object
    description: The value the expression produced
  - name: ids
    type: object
    description: "{ universalId, contentId } — only when Generate IDs is on"
files.node.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/node.schema.json

type: Code
kind: PromiseNode

name: Code
category: Flow
color: "#f59e0b"
logoUrl: https://res.cloudinary.com/sonik/image/upload/v1750052178/gravity/icons/6359572-200.png

description: Execute custom code to transform data

whenToUse: >-
  Transform, reshape, compute or combine data inline with a JS expression: map or filter an array,
  build an object, derive a value from upstream outputs. Prefer it over routing data through an LLM
  node just to reformat or merge it, because it is deterministic and free. Toggle generateIds for
  content hashes, or saveToContext to keep the result reachable from later templates.

# WHO MAY RUN THIS (DECLARATIVE_NODES.md §9.13). Compulsory on every node, so that a node
# nobody thought about cannot look the same as one deliberately left open.
#
# `required: false` adds no requirement of its own: the node runs for whoever the trigger
# admitted. The trigger instance's publicEntry toggle still owns the door, and requirements
# only ever narrow.
auth:
  required: false

capabilities:
  # NOT cacheable: the expression is written over the incoming data, so the same node legitimately
  # answers differently every run. It is also the node most likely to be edited while a workflow is
  # being built, and a cached answer would keep serving the previous version of the code.
  cacheable: false
files.test.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/test.schema.json

# `code` arrives ALREADY RESOLVED — it is a template field the engine evaluates before the node runs —
# so a fixture supplies the finished value, not the expression that produced it. This is the retired
# node's own testData, unchanged, for exactly that reason.
#
# `generateIds` is ON here, which the retired fixture had off. With it off the ids row never fires and
# the fixture proves nothing about the hashes, and the hashes are the only computing this node does.
#
# THE IDS ARE ASSERTED BY SHAPE, not by value, and deliberately. The bench supplies fixed run ids so
# the hashes ARE stable run to run and an exact value could be written down — but pinning one here
# would assert the bench's ids rather than the algorithm, and it would have to be rewritten the day
# the bench changed them. The contentId does not depend on the run at all, and its exact value is
# checked against the retired hashUtils.ts directly rather than through a fixture.

testData:
  config:
    code:
      greeting: hello from Code
      doubled: 42
    generateIds: true
    saveToContext: false
  inputs:
    signal:
      value: 21
  expect:
    # THE VALUE PASSES THROUGH AS AN OBJECT. A resolver that stringified it on the way would still
    # look plausible in a log, so assert the field rather than the whole.
    output: "return output.output.greeting === 'hello from Code' && output.output.doubled === 42"
    # Twelve hex characters each, and the two must DIFFER: they hash different strings (the value
    # alone versus the value keyed by workflow and node), so equal ids would mean one of the two
    # expressions is hashing the wrong thing.
    ids: >-
      return output.ids.contentId.length === 12
        && output.ids.universalId.length === 12
        && output.ids.contentId !== output.ids.universalId
        && output.ids.contentId.split('').every(c => '0123456789abcdef'.includes(c))
